text.en: In 1324, Mansa Musa gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value fell. According to tradition, a year later Tenochtitlan was founded across the world.
Ibn Battuta witnessed the Black Death: in 1348 he was in Damascus, where, he wrote, thousands were dying each day.
Zheng He's first fleet sailed in 1405, 93 years before Vasco da Gama reached India. Later Chinese voyages went as far as East Africa.
The Horde's rule over Rus' ended with the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480 — only 12 years before Columbus reached the Americas.
1492: Granada fell in January, Columbus reached the Americas in October, and in November the Ensisheim meteorite fell in Alsace — one of Europe's oldest witnessed falls.
The Battle of Kulikovo (1380) fell in the middle of the Hundred Years' War, which had been raging for 43 years and had 73 more to go.
Rus threw off the Horde in 1480 and Spain completed the Reconquista in 1492: two centuries-long struggles ended almost together.
Rublev's Trinity (1411 or 1425–1427) and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429) belong to the same generation.
Ivan III's law code (1497) appeared three years after Spain and Portugal divided the world between them at Tordesillas.
Machu Picchu and Gutenberg's press are the same age: around 1450 the Incas were building their mountain estate while Mainz printed its first books.
When Constantinople fell in 1453, Gutenberg was already printing in Mainz: the last Roman Empire vanished in the first years of the printed book.
Korean monks printed the Jikji with movable metal type in 1377, some 70 years before Gutenberg's press.
Mansa Musa made it onto European maps. On the Catalan Atlas of 1375, half a century after his pilgrimage, the ruler of Mali sits on a throne holding a golden nugget.
Mansa Musa said he came to the throne because his predecessor sailed off into the Atlantic. Abu Bakr II wanted to find where the ocean ended, led a fleet west, and never came back.
Ibn Battuta travelled about 117,000 km, almost three times round the equator. In 29 years he went from Morocco to China and from the Volga to Mali, outdistancing Marco Polo.
The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta became chief judge of the Maldives. In the 1340s the island rulers made him qadi; he tried to impose strict laws and soon moved on.
The first quarantine lasted thirty days, not forty. In 1377 Ragusa (Dubrovnik) made arrivals from plague areas wait 30 days; later the period was extended to 40, quaranta in Italian.
After the Black Death, England had to outlaw pay rises. Workers were so scarce that the Statute of Labourers of 1351 ordered wages kept at pre-plague levels.
King Charles VI of France believed he was made of glass. He feared he would shatter, refused to be touched and reportedly had iron rods sewn into his clothes for protection.

The wooden bucket that Modena and Bologna supposedly went to war over has been kept in Modena for some 700 years. It was seized in 1325, and in the 17th century Tassoni mocked the war in his poem "The Rape of the Bucket".
"Drink your blood, Beaumanoir, and your thirst will pass!" So, says the chronicle, a comrade answered the wounded Breton leader who asked for water during the Combat of the Thirty in 1351.

Europe's first woman to make a living as a writer praised Joan of Arc while Joan was still alive. Widowed young, Christine de Pizan supported her family by writing, and in 1429 she wrote a poem on Joan's victories.
Until 1362 English courts spoke French. The Pleading in English Act required cases to be argued in English, because many people no longer understood French.
Robin Hood first appears as the hero of songs known to a lazy priest. In the poem Piers Plowman (around 1377) the priest cannot say his prayers but knows "rhymes of Robin Hood".
Dante booked a place in Hell for a living pope. The Divine Comedy is set in 1300, while Boniface VIII was still alive, and in the Inferno the damned are already expecting his arrival.
In 1409 Catholics had three popes at once. The Council of Pisa deposed the rival popes of Rome and Avignon and elected a third, but the other two refused to go. The schism ended only in 1417.

Friday the 13th is not unlucky because of the Templars. They really were arrested on Friday 13 October 1307, but the superstition is first recorded only in the 19th century, and the Templar link is later still.

In 1386 a sow was tried and executed in Falaise for killing an infant. The hangman was paid for his work and a new pair of gloves; later tales say she was dressed in human clothes. Animal trials were not rare in medieval Europe.

Legend says the maker of Prague's astronomical clock was blinded so he could not build another. But it names Master Hanuš, who only repaired it in 1490; the clock was built in 1410 by Mikuláš of Kadaň and Jan Šindel.
In 1393 the Ming court used 720,000 sheets of toilet paper a year. Each was about 60 by 90 cm, and 15,000 soft, perfumed sheets were made separately for the emperor's family.

The founder of the Ming dynasty had been a beggar. Zhu Yuanzhang was orphaned in the famine of 1344, became a novice monk and wandered the roads with a begging bowl; in 1368 he proclaimed himself emperor.

A Chinese emperor was captured by nomads and later became emperor again. The Oirats seized the Zhengtong Emperor in 1449; freed a year later, he was kept locked up by his brother, and in 1457 he took back the throne.

King Sejong promised that a wise man could learn his alphabet in a morning and a fool in ten days. So says the 1446 book introducing Hangul; before that, Koreans wrote in difficult Chinese characters.
Tamerlane's grandson got the length of the year wrong by just 58 seconds. In 1437 Ulugh Beg in Samarkand calculated the sidereal year as 365 days, 6 hours, 10 minutes and 8 seconds.
The great historian Ibn Khaldun met Tamerlane. In 1401, during the siege of Damascus, he was lowered from the walls by rope and spent weeks in conversation with the conqueror, then wrote it all down.
To take Constantinople, Mehmed II moved his fleet over land. A chain blocked the Golden Horn, so in 1453 some 70 ships were dragged on greased logs over a hill and straight into the harbour.
The guns that smashed the walls of Constantinople were first offered to the Byzantines. The founder Orban approached the emperor, but the treasury could not pay him, so he went to Sultan Mehmed II.
The inventor of printing lost his press in court. In 1455 Gutenberg's creditor Johann Fust won his workshop and his share in the Bible, and the profits went to Fust.
The world's oldest surviving bank was founded in Siena in 1472, twenty years before Columbus sailed. Monte dei Paschi began as a pawnshop meant to protect townspeople from usurers.
In his letter to the Duke of Milan, Leonardo da Vinci mentioned painting only at the very end. Around 1482 he offered Ludovico Sforza bridges, cannons and siege engines, and art "in time of peace".

Leonardo da Vinci's maths teacher is the "father of accounting". In 1494 Luca Pacioli was the first to describe double-entry bookkeeping in a printed book — the debit-and-credit system still used today.

The oldest surviving globe was made in 1492, and America is not on it. Martin Behaim finished his "Erdapfel" in Nuremberg before Columbus returned; between Europe and Asia it shows only ocean and islands.

By the time Columbus sailed, there were probably no Europeans left in Greenland. The last record of its Norse settlers is a wedding in 1408; within decades the colony, which had lasted some 450 years, was gone.
In Calicut, Vasco da Gama's gifts were laughed at. He brought the ruler cloth, hats, coral, sugar and honey, and courtiers said even the poorest merchant from Mecca would offer more.
Chan Chan, capital of Chimor, is the largest city ever built of adobe. The Incas took it around 1470; its mud-brick walls, decorated with fish and birds, still stand.

Haast's eagle hunted moa up to 15 times its own weight. The largest eagle ever known weighed up to 15 kg; the giant flightless birds up to 230 kg. When humans wiped out the moa, the eagle died out too.
The first Lao kingdom was called "A Million Elephants". Lan Xang, founded in 1353, took the name as a boast of military might: elephants were the heavy force of Southeast Asian armies.
Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq ordered Delhi's people to move to a new capital over 1,000 km away. In 1327 much of the population was sent to Daulatabad, and a few years later the capital moved back.

A Delhi sultan issued copper coins worth silver, and his subjects began minting them at home. Around 1330 Muhammad bin Tughluq launched token money; forgeries were so common that he had to redeem them in real silver.
Brunelleschi's dome in Florence and the Aztec Empire are contemporaries. The dome was consecrated in 1436, and the Triple Alliance that created the Aztec Empire formed in 1428, eight years earlier.

Ivan III's bride was married to him by proxy in St Peter's, Rome. Sophia Palaiologina, niece of the last Byzantine emperor, grew up under papal care; the proxy wedding was on 1 June 1472, and she reached Moscow only in November.

Moscow and Mexico City began their rise in the same year: in 1325 Ivan Kalita became Prince of Moscow, and the Aztecs, by tradition, founded Tenochtitlan — the future Mexico City — on an island in a lake.

Russia and China began throwing off Mongol rule at almost the same time. In 1368 rebels drove the Mongols from Beijing and founded the Ming dynasty; twelve years later Dmitry Donskoy defeated Mamai at Kulikovo.
Timur died marching on China in 1405 — the very year China sent its great fleet to sea. The conqueror died at Otrar in February; that summer Zheng He's ships set out on their first voyage.
The Korean alphabet and Gutenberg's press are the same age: King Sejong proclaimed Hangul in 1446, and around 1450 Mainz began printing with movable type.
Two epochs ended in the summer of 1453: the Ottomans took Constantinople in May, and in July the Battle of Castillon ended the Hundred Years' War after 116 years.
A merchant from Tver reached India almost 30 years before Vasco da Gama. Afanasy Nikitin arrived in 1469 and described it in his 'Journey Beyond Three Seas'; the Portuguese got there in 1498.

While Columbus was sailing to America, Italian masters were building the Moscow Kremlin. Its brick walls went up in 1485–1495, so those famous battlements are the same age as the discovery of the New World.
The Ming court mistook a giraffe for the mythical qilin. It reached Nanjing in 1414 with Zheng He’s fleet, and officials congratulated the emperor: a qilin appears only under a sage ruler.
In Japanese and Korean the giraffe is still called “kirin”, the name of the mythical qilin. The mix-up goes back to the giraffe presented to the Chinese emperor in 1414.
The Incas freeze-dried potatoes. Tubers were frozen on high-altitude nights, dried in the sun by day and squeezed out to make chuño, which keeps for years and fed the empire’s armies.
Before 1492 Italy had no tomatoes, Ireland no potatoes, Switzerland no cocoa, and Thailand and India no chilli peppers. All of them came from the Americas after Columbus.

Columbus's critics were right — about size, not shape. Everyone agreed the Earth was round; they argued, correctly, that Asia lay far further west than he claimed. Without the Americas in the way, his crews would have starved.
Medieval people did drink water; beer was not a forced substitute for 'unsafe' water. Towns built wells and conduits, and physicians debated which water was healthiest.
A life expectancy of around 30 did not mean people grew old at 30. High child mortality dragged the average down: medieval people who survived childhood often lived into their sixties or beyond.
Medieval cooks did not use spices to hide rotten meat. Spices were so expensive that anyone who could afford them could certainly afford fresh meat.
Knights were not winched onto their horses. A full suit of plate weighed 15–25 kg spread over the whole body; men in armour could run, vault into the saddle and even do somersaults.
